chunks: Muhammad ibn Musa ibn al-Mutawakkil narrated to me, saying: Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Sa'dabadi narrated to me from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah al-Barqi, who said: My father narrated to us from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Malik ibn Anas from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), from his forefathers (peace be upon them), from the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) who said:

The poor came to the Messenger of Allah and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, the wealthy have what they can free as slaves, and we do not; they have what they can perform Hajj with, and we do not; they have what they can give in charity, and we do not; they have what they can struggle with in jihad, and we do not.' The Prophet said, 'Whoever glorifies Allah a hundred times, it is better than freeing a hundred slaves; whoever praises Allah a hundred times, it is better than leading a hundred camels; whoever says 'Alhamdulillah' a hundred times, it is better than bringing a hundred horses in the path of Allah, with their bridles and saddles and riding them; and whoever says 'La ilaha illa Allah' a hundred times, is the best in deeds on that day, except for someone who does more.' He said: 'The rich heard about this and did the same.' He said: 'The poor returned to the Prophet and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, the wealthy have heard what you said and are doing it too.' He replied, 'That is the favor of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills, and Allah is the possessor of great favor.'

key_terms.فِی سَبِیلِ اللَّهِ: In the path of Allah (for jihad/charity)
key_terms.لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ: There is no god but Allah (Tahleel)

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual reward for reciting Takbir, Tasbeeh, and Tahleel a hundred times compared to material acts of worship?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Thawab al-Amal* highlights the democratization of spiritual merit, offering the poor a superior alternative to the material sacrifices of the wealthy through the recitation of the four key dhikr phrases. Scholarly tradition emphasizes that while the wealthy may perform multiple acts, the consistent devotion of the poor in these verbal remembrances grants them a unique, accessible path to divine favor. The narration concludes by affirming that this spiritual elevation is a specific gift of Allah, underscoring the theme that divine grace is not bound by economic status.
